title: Signals: safe notification and coordinated waiting

opening.title: Signals: an interruption is not an ordinary call
keyPoints: The interrupted code chooses no clean boundary
A handler may interrupt library bookkeeping
Ordinary work should handle the real request
opening.narration: Suppose a process is formatting a status line when a shutdown request arrives. The request did not wait for the formatting library to finish updating its private buffers. That is the central signal problem: the handler can run at an inconvenient point inside ordinary work. A signal is an event notification delivered under operating-system rules. It may request termination, report child changes, or reflect a fault. We must distinguish a routine request from a fault caused by an invalid instruction or memory access. Catching a fault does not establish that the interrupted program is healthy enough to continue. Begin with a minimal notification contract, not a large handler.

question.prompt: Why is calling the usual logging function from a handler risky?
question.answer: It may reenter library state that was interrupted halfway through an update or while holding an internal lock.

opening.title: Choose the promise: request noticed, not events counted
keyPoints: A flag records that work may be needed
Standard signals may coalesce
Normal flow discovers the actual work
opening.narration: A pending notification is not necessarily an exact event count. If several standard signals of the same kind arrive while blocked, they can be represented by one pending instance. A flag set to one therefore means inspect the underlying state, not process exactly one request. For child changes, ordinary code should collect all available child statuses instead of assuming one status for each signal delivery. If every event must carry data and be counted, a queue or another explicit communication mechanism may be needed. The choice comes from the requirement. Replacing a flag with an ordinary increment inside a handler does not create a reliable general event queue.

question.prompt: What should a SIGCHLD-style notification cause the main loop to do?
question.answer: Inspect and collect all available child-state changes under the chosen wait policy, rather than infer an exact count from signal deliveries.

opening.title: Run a minimal real handler
keyPoints: sigaction installs one explicit disposition
The handler only assigns the flag
Output occurs after raise returns
opening.narration: This Linux/POSIX demonstration installs a handler for a signal sent only to the current process. The handler stores one in a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and returns. It does not print, allocate, or take a mutex. raise sends the signal; after successful handling returns, ordinary main prints observed=true. The program checks setup and raise results, and restores the earlier disposition before exiting. This demonstrates real delivery, not an interleaving model. The flag's special type supports this limited handler communication. It is not a replacement for std::atomic in general thread communication, nor does its value tell us how many notifications might have been combined.

question.prompt: Which statement prints, and why is its location important?
question.answer: The std::cout statement in main prints after handling. Keeping stream use outside the asynchronous handler avoids unsafe reentry into stream state.

opening.title: Model the check-then-sleep gap safely
keyPoints: A notification can occur after the check
Sleeping afterward needs another notification
A coordinated check and wait removes that gap
opening.narration: This program is a serialized model, not an actual signal wait. The first path checks a false request flag, then models delivery, then models sleeping because of the stale decision. It prints broken sleeps=true request=true: the request exists while the imagined waiter is asleep. The corrected model makes delivery pending while the decision is protected, then handles it when the coordinated wait enables delivery. Its printed blocked=false means it does not remain asleep after that pending request is handled. No real pause is called, so the demonstration cannot hang waiting for another signal. The model explains why volatile alone cannot combine a check and a later sleep into one operation.

question.answer: It uses the earlier need_to_wait decision after the request has already become true.

mechanism.title: Masks and dispositions answer different questions
mechanism.eyebrow: MASKS AND DISPOSITIONS ANSWER DIFFERENT QUESTIONS
keyPoints: Disposition selects handle, ignore, or default
A thread mask controls delivery eligibility
Blocking delays rather than erases pending state
mechanism.narration: A disposition answers what action a signal should cause. A mask answers whether delivery is currently allowed for a thread. These are different pieces of state, with different scopes in a multithreaded process. Imagine installing a shutdown handler while workers are being created. If masking is part of the plan, establish the intended mask before worker creation and deliberately select who consumes notifications. Otherwise a process-directed signal may reach an eligible worker rather than the thread whose state machine expected it. Blocking an event during setup can preserve it as pending; it does not necessarily throw it away. Describe this lifecycle before adding calls that enable the event source.

question.prompt: Does blocking a signal mean its disposition becomes ignore?
question.answer: No. Masking controls delivery eligibility; the disposition remains a separate action policy.

mechanism.title: sigsuspend links checking with eligibility to wake
mechanism.eyebrow: SIGSUSPEND LINKS CHECKING WITH ELIGIBILITY TO WAKE
keyPoints: Check the predicate while the signal is blocked
Temporarily unblock and wait together
Recheck after each return
mechanism.narration: The correct waiting shape begins by blocking the relevant signal while checking the flag. If work is still absent, sigsuspend temporarily changes the mask and waits in one coordinated operation. A signal already pending can then be delivered without falling into a gap between checking and sleeping. When control returns, the earlier mask is restored and normal code checks the predicate again. A return does not necessarily mean the particular work we want is ready, because another handled signal may be involved. This resembles a condition-variable predicate loop, although its mechanism is a signal mask rather than a mutex. The predicate remains the source of truth.

question.prompt: Why must the flag be checked again after the waiting function returns?
question.answer: The return can be caused by another handled event, and the actual work condition must be confirmed rather than inferred from waking.

mechanism.title: Thread-safe is weaker than signal-safe here
mechanism.eyebrow: THREAD-SAFE IS WEAKER THAN SIGNAL-SAFE HERE
keyPoints: An internal mutex may make ordinary calls safe
The handler may interrupt that mutex owner
Reentering can wait for the interrupted code itself
mechanism.narration: Consider a library routine that locks its private mutex before changing a buffer. Two normal threads can call it safely because one waits for the other. Now imagine a handler interrupts the owning thread and calls that same routine. It waits for a mutex that the interrupted work cannot release until the handler returns. That is why ordinary thread safety does not imply asynchronous signal safety. Keep complex work in normal flow. A self-pipe can bridge a handler to an event loop using a carefully bounded notification write, but a full pipe must not make the handler block. Even a small bridge has a capacity and failure policy.

question.prompt: Why can a mutex-protected library function deadlock when reentered by a handler?
question.answer: The handler can wait for a lock held by the code it interrupted, while that code cannot resume and unlock until the handler returns.

mechanism.title: Restart policy does not erase I/O contracts
mechanism.eyebrow: RESTART POLICY DOES NOT ERASE I/O CONTRACTS
keyPoints: SA_RESTART affects only eligible operations
Interpret each system call’s result
Preserve errno when handler work can change it
mechanism.narration: Installing a handler includes a choice of flags. SA_RESTART can restart some interrupted operations, but it does not promise that every blocking interface behaves as though no signal occurred. I/O code must still examine return values, byte counts, and documented interruption behavior. If a handler calls a permitted operation that may change errno, it may need to save and restore the interrupted value so ordinary error reporting remains meaningful. Keep the roles separate: the handler requests work, the normal operation reports its own progress, and the caller decides whether retrying is valid. Blindly retrying an operation with side effects can be as wrong as blindly treating interruption as fatal.

question.prompt: Does SA_RESTART justify ignoring all interrupted-operation errors?
question.answer: No. Restart behavior is interface-specific, and callers still need to interpret progress and errors under each operation’s contract.

closing.title: Debug a shutdown that is asleep forever
closing.eyebrow: DEBUG A SHUTDOWN THAT IS ASLEEP FOREVER
keyPoints: Record predicate and mask transitions
Look for an unprotected check-then-wait gap
Avoid diagnosing by adding sleeps
closing.narration: A process that stops responding during shutdown may have received the only notification before it actually began waiting. Adding a longer delay can change the symptom without closing the race. Record the sequence instead: when was the flag checked, when was the signal blocked, when did it become pending, and when was delivery enabled? Our safe model gives one concrete failing order. The repair must remove that order from the allowed protocol, not make it unlikely. Also check whether complex handler work is blocked on a library lock. A trace of state and ownership is more useful than a claim that the problem disappeared during ten quiet test runs.

question.prompt: What evidence distinguishes a lost-wakeup problem from simply receiving no request?
question.answer: The request or pending event is present, but the waiter made a stale decision and remains asleep without a future notification.

closing.title: Carry the notification pattern into larger systems
closing.eyebrow: CARRY THE NOTIFICATION PATTERN INTO LARGER SYSTEMS
keyPoints: Minimal handler, durable predicate, normal work
Choose counting separately from waking
Restore process-wide settings when the component ends
closing.narration: A reusable signal component needs more than a successful one-shot example. It must define installation, mask ownership, pending work, restoration of earlier dispositions, and shutdown while other threads still exist. The key lesson transfers to queues and condition variables: a notification says inspect state, while the state records what work remains. If a supervisor needs ten distinct messages, use a protocol that preserves ten messages rather than a flag that merely says yes. If it needs only a shutdown request, the simpler flag may be appropriate. State exactly what the component promises, then test notification before waiting, during waiting, repeated notification, and teardown under that promise.

question.prompt: When is a single flag sufficient?
question.answer: When the requirement is a durable yes/no request, such as shutdown requested, rather than an exact count or payload for every event.
